utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is case IT-96-21-A, the Prosecutor versus Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic, and Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the late commencement. It was caused by some problem with the transportation. Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. My name is Staker. I appear today on behalf of the Prosecution, together with my colleague, Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I'm appearing here on behalf of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is your client here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He is not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tom Kuzmanovic here on behalf of Mr. Mucic. My co-counsel, Howard Morrison, will not be present today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Salih Karabdic, counsel from Sarajevo. I am here with my colleague, Tom Moran, from Houston. We represent Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Cynthia Sinatra, and along with my colleague, Peter Murphy, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Can each of the appellants who are present hear the proceedings in a language which they understand? Mr. Delalic is not here. Mr. Mucic, can you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT MUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT DELIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. This Status Conference has been called in order to comply with the new obligation imposed by Rule 65 bis in relation to appellants who are in custody. Does any counsel wish to raise any issue in relation to the condition of their client who is in custody?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a few matters that I've spoken and discussed with my client about that he would like to bring before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking counsel. That is the usual practice. You tell me what it is you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Landzo suffers from a condition of asthma, and in the detention centre, he is on a smoking floor. There's no segregation between the non-smokers and the smokers. He can't go to the exercise room without being exposed to smoking, and it is detrimental to his physical condition. I understand that there are enough non-smokers and enough smokers with the two floors that they could segregate one floor for non-smokers and one floor for smokers. That's the first issue. The second issue is, I understand that the detention centre is now limiting phone calls home, what's equivalent to a phone card where they can make two calls a week to their family. This segregates the two because the people who have money, that are not indigent, can telephone home all the time. The people who are indigent and in custody are limited to calling their family twice a week. Mr. Landzo has been diagnosed with a psychological condition, and I believe it's detrimental to his psychological condition at this point to not to be able to contact his family. The third issue that we have is that there's a nine-hour time difference between The Hague and California, where his counsel resides, and it's often very difficult to communicate by telephone when he needs to talk to me. So we would ask the Court's permission, and the permission of the U.N. Detention Centre, that if he drafts a letter, that they be allowed to fax it to my office so that I can have the communication from him as soon as possible. Those are the three issues that we have to raise today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have any of these matters been taken up with the commander of the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The smoking issue has been an ongoing issue that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The answer is yes, that one has. Have the other two been?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So far, the commander over there allows me to send faxes to Mr. Landzo but does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please. I did ask you, have these complaints been raised with the commandant. You said one of them has been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: One has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have the other two?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The other two have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, may I suggest that's what you should do. The Tribunal has no power, I have no power to deal with them. If the commandant is unable to deal with them, you may make a complaint to the Registrar, or I think that he has to transfer it to the Registrar. This is an area that's dealt with by the President, and it's not really a matter that I can deal with. So may I suggest that you raise them with the commandant, and if you didn't receive satisfaction, in relation to the smoking one, you take the matter further. But there are regulations, detention regulations, and those should be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other matters by counsel on behalf of their clients?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Tomislav Kuzmanovic, on behalf of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in a way, it relates to our motion for provisional release which had been denied by the Court, and the Court's aware of the timing of the briefing and the fact that, for whatever reason, our brief was not received before the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there was a concession, when it was re-sent, that it would have made no difference. So what is it you want to raise? What's the issue you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It does relate to the condition with respect to my client, Your Honour. His father's standing is such that it is affecting my client's mental state in prison. And the guidance we would seek from the Court, if it's possible, would be, in circumstances the Tribunal has sent medical personnel to check on the status of those to be extradited. Realising that this is a family member, we are seeking the Court's indulgence to try to make a determination of assistance for Mr. Mucic's father -- in a medical situation, for him to be able to have some attempt at, possibly in the future, gaining provisional release to take care of his father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I still don't understand what issue you are raising under Rule 65 bis that I am able to determine. You are not making an application for provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour. We would end up doing it all over again, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, are you asking me to say that the Tribunal should arrange for a medical examination of your client's father?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I have no power to deal with that. That's a matter that has absolutely nothing to do with me. If anybody has anything to do with it, I suggest you proceed through the usual channels out at the detention unit; ask whether some assistance can be given. But I wouldn't promise you that we are going to send people out to look after members of their family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. It does affect my client's condition of imprisonment, simply because it's his father, and I understand the inherent difficulties that the Court has with this issue. But I did want to raise it, since it was an issue. And it is very important to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that, but I really don't see what I can do about it. You will have to make an application to the commandant for some consideration to be given to it and proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Scheduling Order that was issued may perhaps have been understood as suggesting that this was going to be some form of preliminary conference, as the pre-appeal judge in relation to the procedures to be followed for the hearing of the appeal. I really do not think that it is possible to deal with those matters until the deluge of paper ceases. And I see that there was a new filing the other day, for which leave is being sought to file out of time. I do have limited power in the Status Conference to at least note any issues which counsel may wish to raise in relation to the appeal, and I'll return to that in a moment. What I want to do at this stage is to outline to you what this preliminary conference will be when it is held, so that you will be forewarned as to what will be discussed there. There are a number of grounds of appeal which may be described as common grounds, or at least grounds which form a discrete group. An easy one is whether the Bosnian Serbs detained in the Celebici camp were protected persons under the Geneva Conventions. All of the appellants have raised that particular issue. And there is, perhaps, an associated issue, as to whether the conflict in Bosnia at the relevant time was of an international nature. Obviously, it is preferable that such groups -- that such grounds of appeal be argued in a group, and that they be heard completely before moving onto the next group, so that we hear arguments by counsel for the appellants, the response by the respondent, and then a reply, before we move onto the next group. I see that there has been handed in this morning a motion on behalf of three of the appellants. That is obviously the sort of thing which we will be discussing. For what it's worth, I'll tell you how I have roughly grouped them, but I am very happy to hear any suggestions to the contrary. There is the one I've spoken about, about the Geneva Conventions, and whether it's international character of the conflict. Now, the next one, all of the appellants, except Mr. Landzo, have joined in this, where Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute incorporates common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, whether the common article imposes individual criminal responsibility, and whether it applies in international conflicts. And Mr. Delic has raised what might be described as an associated ground, whether the Geneva Conventions apply when Bosnia was not a party to them at the relevant time. Then there are two groups dealing with Judge Odio-Benito, in which all of the appellants, except Delalic, have joined. Whether Judge Odio-Benito was disqualified as a judge at the Tribunal by reason of her election of vice-president of the Republic of Costa Rica, and there has been some further suggestions made in the documents recently filed which are relevant to that. And whether Judge Odio-Benito was disqualified as a member of the Trial Chamber by reason of her membership of the Board of Trustees of the United Nations Voluntary Fund for the Relief of Victims of Torture. And then there is a ground of appeal directed to Judge Karibi-Whyte, in which all, except Delalic, have joined, whether a fair trial was denied by the participation of the Presiding Judge who, it is said, was asleep during substantial portions of the trial. And then all of the appellants, except Landzo, have raised an issue of command responsibility from either of the legal or the factual point of view or both. Then, finally, perhaps what could be called the seventh group, are a number of individual grounds. There are sentencing issues raised by the Prosecution in relation to Mr. Mucic's sentence, Mr. Landzo in relation to his sentence, and there is some further issues raised in the recent filings, if leave is granted to file those submissions. Mr. Mucic has raised the admissibility of the Prosecution interviews and the competence of trial counsel. Mr. Delic has raised the sufficiency of evidence in relation to some of the counts, the issue of nullum crimen, which has been somewhat expanded by the recent submissions, and Mr. Landzo has raised issues of what is described as selective Prosecution and the issue of diminished responsibility. Now, that's the way I see it, but as I say, I am happy to hear, when we come to the preliminary conference, whether you have a better idea of the groupings. I haven't had a chance to read very carefully what was handed in this morning. What I will be seeking to organise, at the preliminary conference, is first the order in which the different groups will be heard. Mr. Delalic, obviously, has only a very limited interest in the whole thing. And his should, obviously, be either first or last, as matters of convenience. And then the order in which we wish the different appellants will be heard in relation to which particular group. What I hope will be agreed between you, but if not agreed, then there is going to have to be some resolution by me, of who is going to be the first counsel in relation to the various groups. Obviously, some -- the way in which the submissions will be made, some have a greater interest in points than others. But the counsel who first addresses will be expected to carry the burden of the argument on that group of grounds of appeal. And counsel who follow will not be permitted to repeat the arguments which the first counsel has put. They will be expected to add anything they wish to add or add material which is directly relevant to their client. Perhaps I should say at this stage that counsel will be required to proceed upon the assumption that the bench is familiar with the written submissions, and we do not want counsel to read their written submissions. Although the bench cannot, of course, promise to be as familiar with those written submissions as counsel are. But we are not there for you to read what we have already read. The second thing to be sorted out at this preliminary conference is the time which counsel estimate their addresses will take. Bearing in mind, once again, that they should not be expected to be allowed to read out their written submissions. The Appeals Chamber will reserve its right to impose time limits which are shorter than the estimates. So I want you, if you will, to start thinking about those matters, and, more particularly, discussing them amongst yourselves, especially in relation to which counsel will carry the burden in relation to the particular groups of grounds of appeal. Now, before I turn to any matters that you want noted, are there any other issues which counsel think could be usefully discussed at the preliminary conference?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Cynthia Sinatra for Esad Landzo. We also have a consideration as far as presentation of evidence. I believe in some of the orders it has been understood that there may be allowed actual live witness testimony prior to the oral argument. We would like some guidance from the Court on what this would entail and how the Court might perceive the presentation of evidence would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was one of the matters that I had noted to discuss under the other part of Rule 65 bis, but I don't mind raising it now. The Prosecution has, I think until next Tuesday, to determine whether it wants to cross-examine the expert on the constitutional law of Costa Rica. But assuming that they do wish to cross-examine the expert, and there is the evidence of Mrs. Sinatra herself, I wondered whether there would be any point in taking that evidence by way of depositions, in advance of the hearing of the appeal. I would like to hear your thoughts about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be taken in one of the courtrooms here, which means that the witness, whoever that witness may be, will be videoed, and if any Judge wants to see it, they will be able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I didn't know whether the Judges would like to participate in the taking of the evidence, because it might be possible, as in my venue, that the Court likes to ask questions of the witnesses at that point. And I don't know whether the Court would have questions that they might like to ask of the expert witness at that point that weren't covered by the Prosecution or the appellant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is your point that you are making that you wish to have the evidence before all four or five Judges?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I understand that. Anybody else have any views about that? Now, you've said that there was an issue as to when it should be taken. Clearly, the evidence would have to be taken before hearing any submissions, but it would depend, would it not, upon the point to which the evidence is relevant. For example, the expert on Costa Rican constitutional law should give his evidence at the beginning of that section of the appeal dealing with the Judge Odio-Benito point. That would be my understanding of the sensible way of looking at it. Have you got anything to say about that? Mrs. Sinatra, you seem to be one of the parties to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am going to defer to Mr. Murphy to discuss the taking of evidence of this expert witness, if the Court will allow so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the most convenient thing, as Your Honour says, it might well to have that evidence taken immediately before the submissions on that issue. There are some other evidentiary issues surrounding what I could call the Judge Odio-Benito grounds which Mr. Staker and I are discussing, and it may well be, Your Honour, that we can resolve those without the necessity for further evidence. Briefly, those are matters which concern the membership of Judge Odio-Benito and the board of trustees, and also the question of whether Judge Odio-Benito accepted ministerial responsibility in the Costa Rican government after the 8th of May 1998. Your Honour, Mr. Staker and I may well be able to resolve that. If not, we should probably be able to deal with it just by putting in certain documents at the same time. So I don't anticipate that will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. In relation to the expert, I suppose that could be dealt with more easily before the five Judges. But what are his movements? He is a lecturer, isn't he, at university?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: He is in private practice, Your Honour. He also teaches. But I'm sure we can arrange for him to attend, as and when necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My idea is that once we know what the estimates are, I would say that on a particular day we will deal with groups one, two, and perhaps three, and the next day groups four, five, six, sort of thing. So we've got at least overnight to get our thoughts together about what's to come the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So when that's sorted out, we can give him some general idea as to when he will be here. Is there anything else about the questions of evidence that are going to arise? Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be responding to the order relating to this expert witness within the required time frame. I just wish to foreshadow at this stage that the Prosecution is giving consideration to the question of whether it should call its own expert witness in relation to the constitutional issues in Costa Rica. That may be an additional factor in assessing procedure. That's, perhaps, a little bit further down the road, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It seems to me that the constitution should speak for itself and that we are there to interpret a document. If there are any cases on -- it's a proper interpretation by the Costa Rican courts, they'd be interesting. But I don't know where all this evidence is leading us, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: There was one very specific issue mentioned in the Prosecution briefs relating to the constitution of Costa Rica, Your Honour, which is one that wasn't addressed in this expert opinion, and that was Villalobos Brenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. Well, then you'll let us know by next Tuesday. Are there any other issues which counsel suggest we should be discussing at this preliminary conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could get a general time frame on when this is going to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the preliminary conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And also the oral argument, Your Honour, so that we can get our schedules straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As I think I've made it clear, the preliminary conference can only take place after we've stopped getting paper from you, so that we can have everything sorted out. The hearing of the appeal, I can't give you any real idea yet. There has to be a further appointment to the Appeals Chamber. But I would say it certainly will not be next month. Hopefully, it will be in April. But that will depend upon what the schedule of the Appeals Chamber is for that month. But certainly the preliminary conference we'll get under way the moment that I can be assured that it is useful to do it, and it's not useful to do it until we know what the grounds of appeal are. Is there any other matter that anybody wants to raise now? Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one further point. I refer to the notice that was filed on behalf of Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic, placing on the record their position that they have joined Mr. Landzo's fourth ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That is not a formal motion, but the Prosecution does expect to respond to it. It does not coincide with their position, and I just wanted to foreshadow at this stage that we would be sending out our position in a written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, at best, they can say they want to amend their grounds of appeal now to rely upon that ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution position, Your Honour, would be that an amendment to the grounds of appeal would require leave of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably so. One of them, in the grounds of appeal, said that they would think about it, as I recall. I've forgotten which one it was. I think they were waiting to see what was going to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That was the brief filed by Mr. Mucic, the original appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And then what are you going to do if they seek leave? I don't want you to say it now, but when you respond to this, it would be best, if I may suggest it, if you say more than just "leave is required." We'd like to know what your attitude towards the grant of leave would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If this leave were applied for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. And I should perhaps also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you can say it's an implied application for leave to amend their grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would also refer to the motion for the filing of the supplementary brief. It would be the Prosecution position that the supplementary brief which is sought to be filed there also appears to raise an additional ground of appeal that hasn't been raised by any of the other appellants before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you're right. From my reading of it, I think you're right, but, no doubt, counsel opposing you from the opposite side of the room will take note of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to raise this issue now. This is something that we will raise at the preliminary hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, are you going to let us into the secret as to what it is about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It will be the issue of my testimony on the issue of waiver, and I didn't know how the Court was going to proceed as far as my presenting evidence on that issue. Will I be asked to give live testimony at that point? Will it be by deposition? What is the recommendation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've just said that you don't want it by deposition, you want it before all five Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you'll have to make up your mind about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That will be prior to the oral arguments, about the same time, is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The three applicants who have filed these further documents -- the three appellants who have filed these further documents, it is true that if you wish to rely upon an additional ground of appeal, leave is required. It may be, on the face of it, an empty formality, but, nevertheless, it's a very important one, so that there is something on the record. Grounds of appeal are of vital importance in the hearing of any appeal so that they define the issues which we are going to decide, and those who wish to rely upon new grounds of appeal arising out of some more recent jurisprudence of the Tribunal should, I think, make it a formal matter, formulate your grounds of appeal, and seek leave to add them. What Mr. Staker says is quite right. What attitude the Appeals Chamber will take will have to resolve at that time. But the sooner the better, that you make your applications. Now, is there anything more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll let Mr. Ackerman have a turn. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. On behalf of Mr. Delalic, I would simply like to urge the Court to reconsider, or continue to consider Mr. Delalic's motion for severance. We have filed everything in that case; it's been ready for argument at the time. It's very painful for Mr. Delalic to sit there with his future in doubt, while all the other people in this appeal continue to bombard the Court with paper. We're prepared to conclude this matter, and would like to do it as soon as possible, and be severed from the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can only say that you've added nothing to what you've already said before, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It means that everybody will have to assemble, and everybody will have to be here, except one party, Mr. Landzo, to determine those issues, and it doesn't save any time or trouble or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My client will be proud of me for having raised it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to raise the issue of timing, and I know that the Court has said that they cannot begin to schedule a preliminary hearing, or the oral argument, until the paperwork stops flowing in. I would like the Court to be apprised that Peter Murphy must begin teaching a course at the end of June, and so we ask that hopefully this scheduling occur in April or May, or the 1st of June, to suit our schedules. I do hope that -- we discussed it last night, everybody met at the same time, and I know that June starts getting hairy for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the amount of pre-appeal activity on this particular appeal has probably broken every record that the Tribunal has ever had. The delay in its hearing has been particularly unfortunate, but, at some stage, I think the Tribunal has to say, "We will not do anything further until you stop bombarding us with paper." It's no good spending a lot of time sorting out what's going to happen in an appeal if everything is then changed by somebody coming along with yet a fresh motion. I think we're up to motion 35, I'm not quite sure about that, but it is absolutely extraordinary. Perhaps if you could exercise some form of control, self-control, a lot of you, we'll get on a lot more quickly. I take note of what you say, and I would be, myself, appalled if this appeal was not heard before June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you for that bit of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. If that's all, thank you for attending, and I'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.05 a.m.
